process: D20: two blind graders (D7), adjudicator on disagreements, agent audit of agreed verdicts (D11)

verdicts.reason: The top-10 share depends on Gartner's IT outsourcing market definition (its denominator). Looked for a public Gartner IT outsourcing market-share release or document abstract for 2008-2009 that states the top-10 share. Wayback CDX holds Gartner 'Market Share Analysis: IT Outsourcing Services, Worldwide' abstracts only from about 2013 on. The Consulting and SI 2010 abstract gives a top-10 share for another segment (32%), which is a different quantity (D23). No measure.

Both readings give miss on the only public ranking found. Literal reading (Japan included): Fujitsu, Hitachi, NTT Data and NEC were all in the global top 20 throughout (Services Top 100 2009 and 2010 editions; Gartner's own 2011 market-share abstract lists Fujitsu and NTT Data among its top vendors), so the count was 4 or more, not one. Dominant reading (Japan excluded): the Services Top 100 ranking of calendar-2008 revenue has none in the top 20 (Huawei 21st, TCS 32nd); the ranking of calendar-2009 revenue has two, Huawei (16th) and Digital China (20th), with TCS 21st. At no point was the count exactly one. Method difference (D23): the Services Top 100 is not Gartner's IT services market-share ranking. It ranks IT services revenue from filings, excluding communication services, but it counts telecom-equipment vendors' IT services, which is how Huawei qualifies. Gartner's own top-20 list for 2007-2010 is not public. Confidence low: on Gartner's definition the ex-Japan count might be one (TCS).

Looked for a 2007-2008 survey measuring the share of data centers that currently lack power or cooling capacity for high-density equipment. Found other quantities. Gartner's December 2007 Data Center Conference poll asked attendees for their top concern: 47% named power availability and 27% insufficient cooling. Emerson's 2009 user-group survey asked when capacity would run out and what limits it (34% power). Both measure concerns or expected limits, not current insufficiency, and neither is a worldwide sample of data centers.

D16 quantitative rule on the US measure. Forecast about 12.2% (2 x 6.1%). Actual 2011: IDC full year 10.73%; Gartner quarters 9.3%, 12.9% (Q3), 11.6% (Q4), annual level about 11%. Error vs forecast 10-14% of the actual (ratio 1.76x-1.82x vs 2.0x): outside the 10% hit band, inside 25%: partial. Western Europe not verified by either grader. Grader A error: its cited MacDailyNews page (2011-10-12) gives no Western Europe share; the 7.6% vs 5.7% figure is not on the page, so A's 'both regions about doubled' is unsupported. A also rounded an about-11% annual US level to 'within 10% of 12%', which holds only at the top of the range.

Edition text now read: the claim is about traveling workers leaving the notebook behind in favour of pocketable devices and web apps. Looked for a 2011-2012 survey of business travelers or mobile workers measuring the share who travel without a notebook. The iPass Mobile Workforce Reports (quarterly, 1,100+ enterprises, 2011-2012) are the closest series; they report devices carried (3.5 devices for work in Q1 2012, 'at least one laptop'), tablet adoption (64%) and desktop abandonment (38%), but never the share leaving the notebook at home on trips. Tablet ownership is a different quantity (D23). No public measure of the stated quantity at 2011-2012.

Looked for a 2011-2012 measure of the share of commercial products containing any open-source component. Found other quantities. Black Duck (November 2009) studied 175+ customers already using open source and found 22% of the average product's code was open source. That is a share of code, from a sample selected for open-source use. Gartner's 2011 survey (cited by HBR) found open source made up 29% of respondents' software portfolios, a share of portfolios. The first codebase-audit figure for the stated quantity (96% of 1,071 audited applications, Black Duck/Synopsys OSSRA) covers 2016, four years after the target, outside the D23 window.

Edition text now read (Sydney release, 2009-02-06): a modelled displacement of seats by telepresence. Seats displaced by telepresence is an attributed value (D23); IATA, ICAO and airline traffic statistics report passengers carried, not seats substituted by video meetings, and no travel-industry body measured the substitution for 2011-2012. Page access does not change this.

Still no public 2012 or 2013 value for this market. Searched for Gartner, IDC (virtual machine software market shares) and trade press figures for 2012-2014. Found only Gartner's 2016 release: $5.6bn in 2016, up 5.7% from about $5.3bn in 2015. If the market grew every year, 2013 was at most about $5.3bn, so the forecast was off by 17% or more and is not a hit. Partial needs 2013 of at least about $4.96bn; miss means less. The bound cannot settle partial against miss, and the 2016 series counts maintenance revenue, which may not match the 2009 basis. IDC's 2013 software release reports segment growth, not this market's size.

The base set is Gartner's 2008 BPO market-share top 20. Looked for it in public form: Gartner's BPO market-share abstracts found start with 2013, and search turned up no public 2008 list. Wayback was offline during this pass, so older Gartner abstracts could not be checked. Known exits in the window: Perot Systems to Dell (2009), ACS to Xerox (2010), Hewitt to Aon (2010), Patni to iGate (2011). With no base list they cannot be counted against the top 20.
Searched for a public IDC, NPD or DisplaySearch statement of the sub-$300 share of worldwide consumer notebook sales in 2011-2012; none found. Price-band splits are in paid trackers only.

No 2012-2013 survey of enterprise knowledge workers on desk phones found. The nearest measure is a RingCentral-commissioned survey of 505 US knowledge workers in May 2015: 83% still had a desk phone, so at most 17% had none. If removals only accumulate, that puts 2013 well under 40%, which would be a miss. But the survey is 18 months after the target, outside the D23 window (target year or the year before), US-only, and vendor-commissioned. Under D23 the claim stays ungradable. The bound is recorded for a dispute or a rule change.

Cited pages do not show the facts the graders rely on: FTC 2014 release gives AT&T throttling from 2011 but no date for ending unlimited sales; AT&T Mobility and Verizon Wikipedia pages give only 2016/2017 reintroduction. No opened source counts how many operators had dropped flat-rate data by 2010 or by 2013-2015, so neither partial nor miss is supported.

A public measure exists: Cisco VNI (May 2013) puts all machine-to-machine traffic, a superset of sensor traffic, at 0.5% of global IP traffic in 2012. Even if non-video traffic were only 40% of IP traffic, M2M would be at most about 1.25% of non-video traffic, an order of magnitude below 20%. An upper bound this far below the forecast settles the claim; it is not a proxy of another quantity (D23). Miss. Grader B's ungradable rested on Cisco VNI being unreachable; the 2013 Cisco release is reachable.

Edition text now read: the claim concerns ownership of IT hardware shifting to third parties (cloud, virtualization, employee-owned PCs). Looked for a 2011-2012 survey of businesses measuring the share that own no IT hardware at all; cloud-adoption and BYOD surveys measure use of some services or devices, not zero ownership, which is a different quantity (D23). No public measure found.

Grader's global figure (eMarketer about $170bn digital ad spend 2015) could not be opened (404); opened pages give only US IAB $72.5bn (2016) and total all-media global ad spend $536-545bn (Magna/Zenith, Breitbart 2014-12-08). Global internet marketing spend could be about $170-200bn, which is miss or partial (within 25% of $250bn) depending on the figure, and the 'regulated' element is not evidenced either way.

Wikipedia Shamoon: 30,000+ Aramco Windows workstations wiped and fuel-truck loading halted, but exploration and production systems were on isolated networks and unaffected, so whether 'critical infrastructure' was damaged depends on the reading. The 2014 German steel mill case is not cited with any source; evidence too weak for hit or miss.

Edition text now read: it narrows the claim to the incentive portion of pay of new G2000 CIOs. CIOs are rarely named executive officers, so proxy filings do not disclose their incentive metrics; no public CIO survey of 2014-2015 reports the basis of incentive pay for this population. No public measure.

Edition text says the claim is about supporting corporate applications on employee-owned notebooks and smartphones, which is what organization-level BYOD surveys measure (organization allows employees to use own devices for work). In-window estimates (2013-2014, D23): Tech Pro Research Feb 2013, 44% of organizations allowing BYOD (18% more planning, 37% vetoed); Tech Pro Research Nov 2014, 74% using or planning to allow, about a quarter ruled out, with currently allowed at 71% for firms of 50-249 staff and 54% for the largest firms reported. Even the upper bound (74%, which includes plans) is 21.6% below 90; currently-allowed shares (44-71%) put 90 more than 25% above the actual. Median of in-window estimates is well under 72, so 90 is beyond 25%: miss under D10. Cisco IBSG 89% 'enable BYOD in some form' is from 2012, outside the target-year window, and not used.

Looked for a 2012-2013 survey of businesses on tablet support. The surveys found measure other things. Forrester and Ovum (2012-2013) give employee shares: 12% of employees use tablets at work; 17.6% have an employer-provided tablet. Dell's IT survey combines offering tablets, supporting them under BYOD and 'thinking about deploying' into one 90% figure, which mixes in intent. Statista's US enterprise tablet series (2013) is paywalled. No measure of the share of businesses supporting a tablet-using workforce.

Edition text now read: cannibalization of current and potential outsourcing revenue by low-cost cloud services. Revenue lost to cloud substitution is an attributed value (D23); outsourcers' filings report total and segment revenue, not revenue cannibalized by cloud, and no tracker publishes that attribution for 2014-2015. 'Up to' also makes the figure a ceiling. No public measure.

Looked for a 2015-2016 survey of enterprise or business email users by primary client. Radicati's Email Statistics Report 2016-2020 executive summary counts business and mobile email users, not users' primary client; radicati.com did not resolve from this session (DNS failure), so the PDF could not be checked. Email-open trackers (Litmus) measure opens of mostly marketing mail across all users, a different population (D23). No measure found.

Public 2016 surveys measure broader populations. Vormetric/451 Research (2016) surveyed 1,100 security executives at 'large enterprises worldwide': 85% use sensitive data in 'the cloud', with public and private cloud not separated. Intel Security (2016, about 2,000 IT professionals at companies of all sizes): 62% store sensitive customer data in the public cloud. Both lean toward the claim, but neither measures the Global 1000, which is the scope the claim names (D23).

Full-year 2014 all mobile phones (Gartner, via Wikipedia table): Samsung 392.5M, Apple 191.4M, Microsoft 185.7M, Lenovo/Motorola 84.0M, LG 76.1M, then Huawei 70.5M: one Chinese vendor in the top five. Full-year 2014 smartphones: Samsung, Apple, Lenovo, Huawei, LG: two. Only the Q4 2014 smartphone quarter (Apple, Samsung, Lenovo, Huawei, Xiaomi) has three. Three Chinese vendors in the full-year top five came in 2015 (smartphones: Huawei 104.1M, Lenovo 72.7M, BBK 72.4M). Not met on the dominant measure in 2014; met on the year-end quarter of a sub-measure and on full-year smartphones one year late: partial, following the late-arrival practice both graders used for event claims. Grader A graded a single-quarter smartphone ranking, a narrower reading than 'handset vendors by year-end 2014'. Grader B reading error: it listed Huawei in the 2014 all-phone top five, but its own figures put LG (76.1M) above Huawei (70.5M), so the count is one, not two.

The claim's cause did not occur: graders themselves record mature-economy employment at record highs by 2019 and no unrest attributed to digitization job loss; the basic-income pilots (Wikipedia UBI pilots: Finland cites automation among several motives) answered anticipated, not realized, labor reduction. D16 gives no partial for half of a compound event whose driver failed, as with 2012-004: miss.

A public measure of fitment exists: in Japan, where low-priced kei cars got low-cost AEB from 2012 (Daihatsu Smart Assist, Mazda SCBS), 41% of new passenger cars sold in 2014 had collision mitigation braking, up from launches in 2012. The direction stated is met by 2014: hit. Caveat: the Japanese figure counts fitment, not only standard fitment. Grader A's ungradable rested on not finding a series; the omitted amount leaves a direction claim, which is gradable. Grader B's citation of UNECE R131 is weak: that regulation covers heavy vehicles, not economy cars; its other evidence (sensor demand, Honda/Toyota announcements) is indirect.

Neither partial rationale is supported: A grades 'done by another agent' (wallets, autofill), which is no D16 test; B's cited Google Assistant page mentions Duplex only for phone calls, not form filling, so the claimed 2019 arrival is unconfirmed. Under the autofill reading it is a hit, under the assistant reading the evidence does not show arrival within 5 years.

Public measures exist. Digital Commerce 360 / eMarketer put mobile at nearly 35% (34.5%) of US e-commerce sales in 2017; comScore put mobile at 21% of total digital commerce dollars in Q4 2016 (the year before). Estimates span 21-35%, a factor under 2 (D23); median about 28%; even the high estimate is 30% below 50%. Miss. Grader A's ungradable was a retrieval gap, not an absence of measures; A itself recalled about one third.

Looked for a count of employees in mandatory tracker programmes in 2017-2018. Every source found describes voluntary or incentive-based wellness programmes. BP America has offered Fitbits since 2013, with about 24,500 users by 2015. In 2018 only 8% of employer wellness plans offered trackers. The West Virginia teachers' plan penalised opting out but did not require trackers. The Christian Science Monitor (March 2018) gives no count of mandatory users. Search results repeat Gartner's own forecast as the only 'two million' figure. No measure.

The only public '100 million consumers shopping with AR' figure (Snap, May 2021) cites 'Gartner Press Release' as its footnote 1. It repeats the forecast and does not measure it. The Deloitte study Snap commissioned measures AR use and attitudes, not a count of AR shoppers. Snap's later figure (250 million Snapchatters used AR shopping lenses since January 2021) covers 2021-2022, one platform, and engagement with any shopping lens; it is not a 2020 measure. No independent count for 2019-2020.

Measured consumption of false news in a mature economy exists: Allen et al. (2020), on a representative US panel of TV, desktop and mobile use, find fake news at 0.15% of the daily media diet and news overall at most 14.2%. For false information to exceed true for most people, the share would have to exceed half; the measured share is orders of magnitude lower, and no later study reports a share near that. Miss. Grader A's Reuters DNR evidence measures concern, not consumption, as A said; but the consumption measure exists, so ungradable does not apply. Data years precede 2022; the gap is too large for the vintage to change the verdict.

The claim states a value attributed to a technology (visits avoided due to AI-enhanced virtual care). Under D23 such an attributed value is ungradable unless a public source measures the attribution; none does (NHAMCS and CDC report total visits, not visits avoided by virtual care). Grader A graded total ED visits (130.0M in 2018, 155.4M in 2022), a different quantity: totals can rise while a counterfactual reduction occurs, so the rise does not establish a miss. A's figures are correct; the reading is the error.

Checked the Global Findex 2025 pages (report hub, accounts/payments chapter, digital-connectivity chapter) and the Little Data Book 2025 PDF: no cryptocurrency or digital-asset measure. Findex covers accounts, mobile money, phone and smartphone ownership. No other survey measures crypto account use among unbanked smartphone owners.

Graded as an adoption claim under D16 (below 5% = miss). The news industry's provenance effort converged on C2PA (founded with BBC, Microsoft, Adobe, and the New York Times' involvement), which secures provenance with hash codes and certified digital signatures, not a blockchain. Blockchain authentication of news stayed at pilot or single-outlet scale, which bounds the share far below 5% of world news and video. No survey gives a share, but adoption at this scale is evident from what was deployed, as for other D16 adoption calls; ungradable would require that no measure of the claim's state exists. Least certain call in this set on the ungradable boundary.

The claim names its own measure, a CEO survey. Gartner's 2024 CEO and senior executive survey (416 respondents) reports top business priorities with shares (growth 62%, then technology and workforce); content moderation is not among the reported priorities, so its share is well below 30%. Miss. The survey release itself returned 403 and the archive was blocked; the priority list is from search summaries cited by grader B. Grader A looked for the item and found it absent, which is evidence of a miss rather than of no measure.
